first.rationale: Simplifying onboarding directly addresses the 4% completion decline and may also recover activation while avoiding the margin and customer-quality risks of reacting immediately with discounts. Verify memory_86 for durability and qualified-revenue effects, and memory_73 to assess whether promotional pricing produced durable revenue rather than only short-term acquisition. Start guarded because prior evidence emphasizes adoption proxies more than long-term qualified revenue.

mid.rationale: Run a standard experiment shortening onboarding. The verified source directly addresses the current 4% completion decline and showed completion +13%, time-to-value improved by 2.1 days, and 30-day retention +3%, supporting sustainable adoption. Signup simplification provides related evidence that reducing friction can lift activation. Reject promotional pricing this cycle: despite +18% qualified revenue initially, its cohort had 30-day retention down 12% and failed to survive renewal. Measure activation, qualified revenue, and retention guardrails because evidence beyond 30 days remains limited.

final2.rationale: Proceed with the shortened-onboarding experiment despite the competitor's deeper price cut. Verified evidence shows improved completion, faster time-to-value, and higher 30-day retention, directly addressing current onboarding and activation deterioration. Do not react with promotional pricing: the verified 40% discount generated short-term qualified revenue but reduced 30-day retention by 12% and failed at renewal, conflicting with the sustainable-revenue objective. Track price-sensitive SMB churn and qualified revenue as guardrails; the new competitive pressure may reduce the historical effect size.
